specPoints.text: be able to calculate the rate of a reaction from: i the time taken for a reaction, using rate = 1/time ii the gradient of suitable graph, by drawing a tangent, either for initial rate, or at a time, t

primer.text: Rate is a gradient wearing units. This note teaches the tangent craft on product-versus-time curves, then tours the lab methods - mass loss, gas syringes, disappearing crosses and quenched titrations - with each method's strengths and its sampling traps laid bare.

lessons.title: Reading rate from graphs and tangents
lessons.opening: Rate is a gradient in disguise: plot amount against time and the steepness of the curve speaks the reaction's speed. Draw a tangent, read the triangle, divide - that is the whole craft of instantaneous rate.
keyPoints: Rate of reaction has units mol dm-3 s-1 and equals the change in amount of reactant or product divided by time.
As a reaction proceeds, reactant concentration falls and product concentration rises.
On a graph, rate at a moment is the gradient of a tangent to the curve at that time.
A large tangent triangle reaching gridlines minimises reading error.

low.restatement: Steep early, flat late: the curve's gradient falls as reactants are consumed. The tangent's triangle (change in y over change in x) converts steepness into a rate number with units.
low.analogy: A slide that starts steep and flattens near the bottom: your speed is the slope where you stand, read from how much height you lose over how much ground.
low.examPointer: Draw the tangent with a large triangle crossing gridlines, then compute change in y divided by change in x - small triangles magnify misreads.

medium.restatement: The instantaneous rate is a derivative read graphically: tangent gradient at the chosen time. Concentration axes give mol dm-3 s-1; gas volume axes give cm3 s-1. The curve flattens because reactant depletion throttles successful collisions.
medium.analogy: The curve is a road; the tangent is your compass heading at one instant, and the triangle is the map square you use to measure the heading.
medium.examPointer: State units explicitly - a bare number loses the mark; pick the units the axes demand.

check.stem: Rate of reaction is defined as

options.text: The change in amount of reactant or product per unit time
options.explanation: Rate quantifies how quickly concentration shifts, in mol dm-3 s-1.

options.text: The total amount of product made before the reaction stops
options.explanation: That is the yield, not the rate.

options.text: The time a reaction takes from start to finish
options.explanation: That is duration; rate divides change by that time.

options.text: The gradient of the reactant curve multiplied by time
options.explanation: The gradient IS the rate; no extra multiplication applies.

check.stem: On a graph of product volume against time, the reaction is fastest

options.text: Where the curve is steepest, usually at the start
options.explanation: Steepest gradient means most product forming per second.

options.text: Where the curve flattens near the end
options.explanation: A flat curve signals reactants exhausted and rate near zero.

options.text: At the point of maximum volume
options.explanation: Maximum volume is the endpoint, where rate has fallen to zero.

options.text: Anywhere, since rate is constant throughout
options.explanation: Rates decline as reactants are consumed.

check.stem: A tangent drawn at 20 seconds gives the rate

options.text: At exactly 20 seconds, the instantaneous rate
options.explanation: The tangent's gradient reads the speed at that single moment.
The average rate comes from endpoint-to-endpoint gradients, not tangents.

options.text: At the start of the reaction
options.explanation: Only if the tangent touches at time zero.

options.text: At the end of the reaction
options.explanation: The tangent location sets the time, which is 20 seconds here.

check.stem: Why should the tangent triangle be large?

options.text: Large triangles reach gridlines, reducing misreads of both axes
options.explanation: Bigger spans shrink relative reading error in the gradient.

options.text: Large triangles make the curve steeper
options.explanation: The curve's steepness is fixed; the triangle only measures it.

options.text: Small triangles are not allowed by examiners
options.explanation: Size guidance is about accuracy, not a ban.

options.text: The tangent only exists for large triangles
options.explanation: A tangent is a line; triangle size is a measuring choice.

check.stem: As reactants are used up, the curve of product against time

options.text: Becomes less steep because successful collisions become rarer
options.explanation: Falling reactant concentration throttles the collision-driven rate.
Accumulated products do not accelerate the forward reaction here.
A straight line would mean constant rate, which does not hold.
Product volume is positive and rising.

check.stem: State the units of rate of reaction when concentration is plotted.
check.modelAnswer: Mol dm-3 s-1, concentration change per second.

check.stem: Describe how to find the rate at a given time from a curve.
check.modelAnswer: Draw a tangent to the curve at that time, complete a large triangle, and divide the change in y by the change in x.

check.stem: Explain why the rate decreases as the reaction proceeds.
check.modelAnswer: Reactant concentration falls, so collision frequency drops and fewer successful collisions occur per unit time, flattening the curve's gradient.

check.stem: A tangent at 20 s spans 24 cm3 vertically and 40 s horizontally. State the rate with units.
check.modelAnswer: Rate = 24 / 40 = 0.60 cm3 s-1 at the 20-second mark.

lessons.title: Measuring rate by mass loss
lessons.opening: Let the gas carry the mass away: a balance under the reaction vessel tracks how much product escapes per second. Simple, but only for dense gases - light hydrogen barely dents the reading.
keyPoints: When a gas escapes the vessel, mass decreases, so mass loss over time measures rate.
Calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid releases CO2, mass being recorded every few seconds.
The mass-loss graph is equivalent to amount of reactant against time.
The gas must be dense enough; CO2 (Mr 44.0) registers, hydrogen (Mr 2.0) does not.

low.restatement: Mass loss is a product meter: each escaping gram marks progress. Dense gases move the balance visibly; Mr 2.0 hydrogen disappears into rounding noise.
low.analogy: A leaky water tank on a scale: heavy drips show clearly, faint mist does not.
low.examPointer: Justify gas choice by molar mass when asked why hydrogen is unsuitable for mass-loss rate experiments.

medium.restatement: The balance converts a concentration change into a mass signal without touching the mixture; the trade-off is sensitivity limited by the gas's molar mass and balance resolution (2-3 decimal places).
medium.analogy: Watching a truck leave a car park by weighbridge works; watching a cyclist leave does not register.
medium.examPointer: Name 'gas must be sufficiently dense' as the limitation, quoting Mr values 44.0 versus 2.0.

check.stem: A balance under the reaction vessel can time a rate because

options.text: Escaping gas lowers the vessel's mass proportionally to product formed
options.explanation: The balance tracks product escape as a mass signal over time.
Mass is measured; concentration is inferred.

options.text: All gases have large molar masses
options.explanation: Hydrogen's Mr 2.0 is far too light to register reliably.
The method relies on gas leaving, not staying.

check.stem: Hydrogen production is poorly tracked by mass loss because

options.text: Its molar mass is only 2.0, too small for a 2-3 d.p. balance
options.explanation: Tiny mass changes vanish below the balance's resolution.

options.text: Hydrogen is not produced in reactions
options.explanation: Plenty of reactions produce hydrogen.
No such interference exists.
It escapes readily; the reading simply barely moves.

check.stem: In the CaCO3 + HCl experiment, the mass is recorded

options.text: Every few seconds as the CO2 escapes
options.explanation: Frequent sampling captures the falling mass curve.
A single reading gives no rate.
The starting mass is the baseline, not the rate data.
Sealing would stop the mass loss the method depends on.

check.stem: The mass-loss graph mirrors a graph of

options.explanation: Mass lost equals reactant consumed, so the shapes correspond.
Unrelated axes for this method.
No volume axis appears in mass loss.
Catalyst mass does not change.

check.stem: Which product gas registers on the balance in a mass-loss experiment?

options.explanation: Dense enough to shift a sensitive balance measurably.
Far too light for reliable mass readings.

options.text: Any gas, since all are weighed equally
options.explanation: Molar mass decides the signal size.
The method targets product gas escape such as CO2.

check.stem: State one limitation of the mass-loss method.
check.modelAnswer: The gas must be sufficiently dense; a light gas like hydrogen changes the mass too little to measure.

check.stem: Name a reaction suitable for the mass-loss method.
check.modelAnswer: Calcium carbonate reacting with hydrochloric acid, which releases carbon dioxide.

check.stem: Explain why the mass-loss curve flattens as time passes.
check.modelAnswer: Reactant depletion lowers the rate, so less gas escapes per second and the mass stops dropping steeply.

check.stem: A student records 0.12 g lost in the first 30 s and 0.02 g in the next 30 s. Comment on the rate change and its cause.
check.modelAnswer: The rate fell from about 0.004 g s-1 to about 0.0007 g s-1: acid is being consumed, so fewer successful collisions occur and gas escapes more slowly.

lessons.title: Measuring rate by gas volume
lessons.opening: Trap the gas and time its growth: a syringe or an inverted cylinder over water turns product formation into a rising volume curve. Volume is a product meter, read every few seconds into a graph whose gradient is the rate.
keyPoints: Trapping the product gas and reading its volume as time passes gives a rate signal.
Magnesium with hydrochloric acid produces hydrogen, collected by gas syringe or inverted cylinder.
The inverted measuring cylinder works when the gas is not water-soluble.
The volume graph plots amount of product against time, and its gradient is the rate.

low.restatement: Collected volume climbs steeply early, flattening as reactants thin out; each reading marks cumulative product, and the gradient between readings is the rate.
low.analogy: Filling a bath from a tap that slows down: early marks rise fast, late marks crawl.
low.examPointer: Choose the syringe for soluble gases; the inverted cylinder only when the gas is not water-soluble.

medium.restatement: Gas volume translates stoichiometry into observable progress without sampling the mixture; it measures the product side directly, complementing mass loss's reactant view. Water solubility decides the collection apparatus.
medium.analogy: A growing balloon taped to a ruler: every centimetre is product made so far.
medium.examPointer: State 'not water-soluble' as the condition for the inverted-cylinder variant - the examiner checks that qualification.

check.stem: A gas syringe measures rate by recording

options.text: The volume of gas produced at intervals of time
options.explanation: Volume growth over time is the product meter of this method.
That is the mass-loss method's signal.
Volume, not pressure, is the recorded variable here.
Sampling concentration is a different, harder method.

check.stem: The inverted measuring cylinder setup is appropriate only when

options.text: The gas is not soluble in water
options.explanation: Soluble gas would dissolve into the water instead of collecting.
Enthalpy change is irrelevant to collection choice.

options.text: The gas is denser than air
options.explanation: Displacement direction is not the stated criterion.
Colour is irrelevant to volume collection.

check.stem: In the Mg + HCl experiment, the volume-time graph's gradient gives

options.explanation: Volume per second is the rate of product formation.
Ea needs a different analysis entirely.
The final plateau gives yield; the gradient gives rate.
Acid concentration is a set condition, not read from this graph.

check.stem: Which collected gas is measured by volume over time?

options.text: Mg + HCl hydrogen by gas syringe; CaCO3 + HCl CO2 by either method
options.explanation: Hydrogen suits syringe; CO2 works by syringe or inverted cylinder.

options.text: Hydrogen by inverted cylinder over water
options.explanation: Hydrogen is barely soluble, so cylinder works too - but the classic pairing is syringe.

options.text: CO2 by inverted cylinder over water only
options.explanation: CO2 can also be collected cleanly by syringe.
O2 (Mr 32) could register by mass, but the stated pairing is wrong.

check.stem: Volume measurement offers which advantage over mass loss?

options.text: It tracks light gases such as hydrogen effectively
options.explanation: Volume responds to moles, so Mr 2.0 hydrogen registers perfectly.
Syringes and cylinders are apparatus.
Volume data is graphed exactly like mass data.
Volume reads the product side.

check.stem: State the condition for using an inverted measuring cylinder over water.
check.modelAnswer: The collected gas must not be soluble in water.

check.stem: Name the gas and reagents in the classic gas-volume rate experiment.
check.modelAnswer: Magnesium with hydrochloric acid producing hydrogen gas.

check.stem: Explain why the volume curve rises steeply then flattens.
check.modelAnswer: Early on, high reactant concentrations give frequent successful collisions and fast gas evolution; as reactants deplete, the volume gain per second shrinks.

check.stem: A syringe reads 18 cm3 at 10 s and 42 cm3 at 30 s. Estimate the average rate in that window with units.

lessons.title: Concentration changes, quenching and the disappearing cross
lessons.opening: Sampling concentration mid-reaction is invasive - unless you quench, freezing the chemistry for titration. Often it is easier to stop the clock at a visible endpoint, as the thiosulfate-sulfur cross does, at the cost of a single data point.
keyPoints: Taking and titrating samples can disturb the rate unless the reaction is deliberately stopped, called quenching.
It is often convenient to time a visible endpoint, such as magnesium dissolving completely in acid.
Sodium thiosulfate with hydrochloric acid slowly forms yellow sulfur that hides a cross beneath the flask.
The endpoint method's main limitation is that it yields only one piece of data.

low.restatement: Quenching halts the sampled aliquot so titration reads a true concentration; endpoint timing trades many data points for one clean visible moment.
low.analogy: Freezing a scoop of soup to test its heat versus watching for the crouton to sink - one is precise and invasive, the other quick and single-shot.
low.examPointer: Name quenching explicitly and state the one-data-point limitation of cross experiments.

medium.restatement: The disappearing cross couples rate to turbidity: sulfur colloids scatter light until the printed cross vanishes, and that fixed endpoint time compares rates across conditions. Consistency of judgement (same cross, same eye) is the hidden control.
medium.analogy: A fogged window: you time how long the garden takes to blur beyond recognition - the same window, the same criterion, every run.
medium.examPointer: Quote the thiosulfate equation with its sulfur product when describing the classic experiment.

check.stem: Quenching a reaction sample means

options.text: Deliberately stopping the reaction in the sample so it can be analysed
options.explanation: The stopped aliquot preserves the concentration snapshot for titration.

options.text: Cooling the apparatus with ice water
options.explanation: Cooling is one quenching tactic, but quenching means stopping the reaction.

options.text: Adding more reactant to speed up
options.explanation: That changes the reaction, not the sample.
Filtration is separation, not reaction stopping.

check.stem: The sodium thiosulfate + hydrochloric acid experiment times

options.text: How long the yellow sulfur precipitate takes to hide a cross under the flask
options.explanation: Turbidity growth is the clock of the disappearing cross.

options.text: How long the acid takes to evaporate
options.explanation: No evaporation is involved.
Only the visibility endpoint is timed.
The reaction is not monitored by temperature here.

check.stem: The main limitation of endpoint timing is

options.text: It produces only one data point per run
options.explanation: A single time trades resolution for simplicity.
A flask, paper cross and stopwatch suffice.
Comparing endpoint times across conditions is its main use.
Nothing radioactive appears.

check.stem: Why can taking samples for titration disturb a rate measurement?

options.text: Sampling and analysing can affect the reaction rate unless the sample is quenched
options.explanation: Removing reactant and changing temperature perturb the remaining mixture.

options.text: Titrations are too slow for any rate work
options.explanation: Quenched aliquots are standard rate tools.
The perturbation is mechanical and thermal, not indicator chemistry.

options.text: Samples cannot be removed from flasks
options.explanation: They can, with pipettes.

check.stem: Na2S2O3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + SO2 + H2O + S shows sulfur as

options.text: A yellow precipitate responsible for the cloudiness
options.explanation: Colloidal sulfur scatters light until the cross disappears.
SO2 is the gaseous product; sulfur stays put.
The sulfur is the visible insoluble colloid.
Sulfur is a product, not a catalyst.

check.stem: Define quenching.
check.modelAnswer: Deliberately stopping a reaction, typically in a removed sample, so its concentration can be measured faithfully.

check.stem: State what is timed in the disappearing cross experiment.
check.modelAnswer: The time until the yellow sulfur precipitate obscures a cross drawn under the flask and viewed from above.

check.stem: Explain why endpoint timing suits condition comparisons despite its limitation.
check.modelAnswer: Because every run shares the identical endpoint criterion, the reciprocal of the recorded time provides a comparable rate index across concentrations or temperatures.

check.stem: Halving the thiosulfate concentration lengthens the cross time. Explain with collision theory why the clock slows.
check.modelAnswer: Fewer thiosulfate particles per volume lowers collision frequency with acid, so sulfur forms more slowly and the turbidity reaches the cross-hiding threshold later.

glossary.definition: A straight line touching a curve at one point whose gradient equals the instantaneous rate there.
Deliberately stopping a reaction in a removed sample so its concentration can be analysed faithfully.
The rate at time zero, found from the tangent drawn at the start of the curve.

workedExample.prompt: The iodine-methanoic acid reaction releases carbon dioxide, plotted as volume against time. Using the tangent at the 20-second mark, find the rate.
steps: Draw the tangent to the curve at 20 seconds, extending it to cross gridlines.
Complete a large right triangle on the tangent and read off the change in y and change in x.
Divide: rate = change in y / change in x = 24 / 40.
Attach units from the axes: volume in cm3 over time in seconds.
